cards.title: Polynomial-time minimum-total-length disjoint paths for fixed k
cards.formal: For every fixed integer \(k\ge 3\), is there a polynomial-time algorithm that, given an undirected unweighted graph G and k prescribed terminal pairs \((s_{i},t_{i})\), outputs pairwise vertex-disjoint paths \(P_{i}\) from \(s_{i}\) to \(t_{i}\) minimizing \(\sum _{i}|E(P_{i})|\), or correctly reports that no such collection exists? Randomized algorithms with success probability at least \(2/3\) on every input are admitted in this reading, consistently with the randomized \(k=2\) baseline cited by the source. Polynomial degree and constants may depend on k; an FPT bound with exponent independent of k is not requested.
cards.definitions: G is a finite simple connected undirected graph with n numbered vertices and unit length on every edge, encoded by an adjacency matrix and the terminal labels. Take the 2k terminals to be distinct; repeated endpoints across different pairs make vertex-disjointness infeasible, and a pair with \(s_{i}=t_{i}\) uses the zero-edge path at that vertex and can be handled separately. A path is a sequence of distinct vertices with consecutive vertices adjacent. Vertex-disjointness includes endpoints and means \(V(P_{i})\cap V(P_{j})=\varnothing\) for \(i\ne j\). Pairings are fixed: connecting a source to a different pair’s target is not acceptable. Define OPT as the minimum sum of edge counts over all feasible collections and set OPT=∞ when there is none. The output consists of the k vertex sequences of an optimal collection, or an infeasibility answer. For each fixed k the algorithm is a probabilistic Turing machine, with one finite program handling all n and all inputs for that k, running in at most \(C_{k}(n+1)^{c_{k}}\) steps on every random-bit sequence. Constants \(C_{k},c_{k}\) are independent of n. With probability at least \(2/3\) over its independent fair bits, the full output must be correct, including exact optimality. A deterministic algorithm is included as the zero-error case. The formulation asks for polynomial time for each fixed k and does not demand a uniform procedure generating these programs as k varies. The source compares this target with k-DSP, which requires every \(P_{i}\) separately to have length \(\operatorname{dist}_{G}(s_{i},t_{i})\). Such a collection, when it exists, has the smallest possible total length; minimum-total-length routing must also handle inputs where disjoint routes exist but no collection of individually shortest routes exists.
cards.answer_criterion: Establish or refute polynomial-time solvability, with the stated bounded-error allowance, for every fixed \(k\ge 3\). A positive answer must output an exactly optimal collection or detect infeasibility on all inputs. A negative answer must exclude every allowed bounded-error polynomial-time algorithm for at least one fixed \(k\ge3\). Any additional hypothesis used to prove this exclusion must itself be established. Hardness only when k grows with n, an FPT lower bound, approximation, or an algorithm restricted to individually shortest paths does not decide this question.
cards.why: Would determine whether exact length optimization preserves the polynomial-time solvability of undirected disjoint routing with a fixed number of prescribed terminal pairs.

cards.title: Linear-size sample compression
cards.formal: Is there a universal integer \(C\ge1\) such that every nonempty Boolean concept class \(H\subseteq\{0,1\}^{X}\) on an arbitrary set \(X\), with finite VC dimension \(d\ge1\), admits a labeled sample compression scheme with nonnegative integer kernel and side-information bounds \(k,b\) satisfying \[k+b\le Cd?\] The scheme is exact on every finite \(H\)-realizable sample, stores an unordered subset of labeled sample records plus \(b\) bits, and may reconstruct a predictor outside \(H\). Its compressor, reconstructor, \(k\), and \(b\) may depend on the complete class, but the same scheme and bounds must work for all sample sizes. Only \(C\) must be universal. This preserves the card’s previously selected linear-size, counted-side-information formulation.
cards.definitions: A concept is a total Boolean function on \(X\). A finite set \(U\subseteq X\) is shattered by \(H\) if \(\{h|_U:h\in H\}=\{0,1\}^{U}\); the VC dimension is the largest cardinality of a shattered set. A finite labeled sample is a finite set \(S\subseteq X\times\{0,1\}\). It is \(H\)-realizable if some \(h\in H\) agrees with every pair in \(S\); in particular, a realizable sample has no contradictory labels at the same point. The empty sample is allowed. A scheme consists of deterministic set maps \(\kappa\) and \(\rho\). For every realizable \(S\), \(\kappa(S)=(T,z)\), where \(T\subseteq S\), \(|T|\le k\), and \(z\in\{0,1\}^{b}\). The reconstruction \(\rho(T,z):X\to\{0,1\}\) is a total predictor satisfying \[\rho(\kappa(S))(x)=y\qquad\text{for every }(x,y)\in S.\] The reconstructor is defined for all possible finite labeled kernels of size at most \(k\) and all \(b\)-bit strings, with consistency required only on actual compressed messages. It receives no original sample, sample size, omitted point, original index or ordering of retained examples. One retained labeled example costs one unit, even on a domain whose points have no finite binary descriptions; each side-information bit costs one unit. The retained set is unordered. A finite side alphabet \(I\) instead of bit strings costs \(\lceil\log_2|I|\rceil\) bits. Allowing variable-length strings of bounded length changes this linear-size question only by a constant factor if their lengths are encoded as part of the message. The compressor is required only on realizable samples. Reconstruction need not be proper, stable under deletion of unused records, computable, efficient, or measurable. No randomness or data-distribution promise is involved. Dimension zero is omitted from the display because a nonempty such class has one pointwise labeling and admits a scheme storing nothing. All classes of positive finite dimension, not just finite domains or finite classes, are included.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a Lean-checked proof of the stated universal linear bound, or of its logical negation. A positive answer must provide a single universal constant and, for each class, a valid compressor and reconstructor with the counted size bound holding on every realizable sample. A negative answer must show that for every integer \(C\ge1\), some class of positive finite VC dimension admits no such scheme of size at most \(Cd\). A lower bound against only proper, stable, efficient, or otherwise restricted reconstruction does not refute this unrestricted target. Neither does failure of a particular embedding construction. Free side information or free ordering of retained points is outside the model. The requirement is exact consistency and linear size with a universal constant; it asks for no additive numerical approximation.
cards.why: A central question connecting the combinatorial complexity of prediction with how many observations suffice to represent all training decisions. Its universality across concept classes, and its links to learning, extremal set systems and graph geometry, make the linear-versus-exponential gap fundamental.

cards.context:
The compressed object lets a fixed decoder reproduce every label in the original training sample. It need not identify the unknown target on points that were never observed. The same decoder must work at every sample size, so a bound depending only on the class’s VC dimension would be independent of how much training data was supplied.

The distinction between examples and bits is essential. A domain point may require arbitrarily many bits to describe, but sample compression charges one unit for retaining its labeled record. Conversely, an unbounded uncharged message would evade the intended resource bound. Both the retained kernel and the side information are therefore limited explicitly, and the kernel has no free ordering.

Moran and Yehudayoff prove that every binary class of VC dimension \(d\) has a scheme of total size \(2^{O(d)}\). Their sharper theorem also depends on dual VC dimension, which exchanges the roles of domain points and hypotheses by regarding a point as its vector of labels across the class. That dual dimension can grow exponentially in \(d\), leaving the general linear-versus-exponential gap. The checked result is from the corrected v2 and subsequent journal publication.

Chase and coauthors show that some finite classes require an exponential increase in dimension to be contained in an extremal class, a structured type of class with known tight compression. This limits a previously studied embedding-based route to compression. It does not prove that the original class itself requires an exponential-size scheme.

The April 2026 graph-ball paper explicitly retains the general linear conjecture. It gives proper compression of size \(O(t\log(t+1))\) for graph-ball classes whose underlying graph has treewidth at most \(t\), and an analogous cliquewidth result. The predictors are themselves balls, but the resource parameter is graph width and the family is restricted. These structured results are not a universal linear-VC theorem.

The 2025 reduction paper transfers some binary compression bounds to multiclass, regression and robust-learning settings. The sharper transfers need additional reconstruction or stability properties. The ordinary linear conjecture appears in its introduction; its later robust-compression open problem is a different target.

A March 2026 preprint first claimed a sample-compression breakthrough and later a no-clash teaching result. The current checked version, dated 3 August 2026, is withdrawn and identifies an incorrect proof of Lemma 2. Its stale search-result title and earlier abstract are not evidence that the conjecture has been resolved.

cards.title: NPT bound entanglement
cards.formal: Does there exist a negative-partial-transpose state that is undistillable for every finite number of copies? Precisely, are there integers \(a,b\ge2\) and a density matrix \(\rho\) on \(\mathbb C^a\otimes\mathbb C^b\) such that \(\rho^{\Gamma_B}\) has a strictly negative eigenvalue and \[\langle\psi,(\rho^{\Gamma_B})^{\otimes k}\psi\rangle\ge0\] for every integer \(k\ge1\) and every unit vector \(\psi\in(\mathbb C^a)^{\otimes k}\otimes(\mathbb C^b)^{\otimes k}\) of Schmidt rank at most two across the displayed bipartition? The same dimensions and the same state must satisfy the condition for all \(k\).
cards.definitions:
All vector spaces are finite-dimensional over \(\mathbb C\). The inner product is \(\langle u,v\rangle=\sum_j\overline{u_j}v_j\), and a unit vector has \(\langle u,u\rangle=1\). A density matrix \(\rho\) is Hermitian, positive semidefinite and of trace one: \(\rho=\rho^\dagger\), \(\langle v,\rho v\rangle\ge0\) for every vector \(v\), and the sum of its diagonal entries is one. Dagger denotes conjugate transpose. In the fixed standard product basis, with indices \(i,r\in\{1,\ldots,a\}\) and \(j,s\in\{1,\ldots,b\}\), its partial transpose on the second party is \[(\rho^{\Gamma_B})_{(i,j),(r,s)}=\rho_{(i,s),(r,j)}.\] This matrix is Hermitian but need not be positive semidefinite. Negative partial transpose, abbreviated NPT, means it has an eigenvalue strictly less than zero. Positive partial transpose, abbreviated PPT, means all its eigenvalues are nonnegative; zero eigenvalues do not make a state NPT. The \(k\)-fold tensor power is the Kronecker product of \(k\) copies of the same matrix. When evaluating the displayed expectation, regroup the tensor factors from \((A_1B_1)\cdots(A_kB_k)\) into \((A_1\cdots A_k)(B_1\cdots B_k)\), where \(A_j=\mathbb C^a\) and \(B_j=\mathbb C^b\). The corresponding permutation of basis vectors is part of this identification. Schmidt rank of \(\psi\) across these two groups is the least integer \(r\) such that \(\psi=\sum_{j=1}^r u_j\otimes v_j\), with \(u_j\in(\mathbb C^a)^{\otimes k}\) and \(v_j\in(\mathbb C^b)^{\otimes k}\). No independence or product condition is imposed between copies within either party.

A bipartite state is separable if it is a finite convex combination \(\sum_j p_j\sigma_j\otimes\tau_j\) of local density matrices, with \(p_j\ge0\) and \(\sum_jp_j=1\); otherwise it is entangled. Every NPT state is entangled. The exact criterion used in this question defines \(k\)-copy distillability as existence of a Schmidt-rank-at-most-two unit vector with strictly negative displayed expectation. A state is distillable if such a vector exists for at least one finite \(k\); undistillable means none exists at any finite \(k\). This finite-matrix definition is the formal target. It agrees with the standard operational notion of obtaining entangled two-qubit states with positive probability from finitely many copies using local operations and classical communication, and hence of distilling Bell pairs at positive asymptotic rate. That interpretation allows two-way classical communication and local ancillary systems, but no quantum communication or extra shared entanglement. The card asks for mathematical existence, not efficient preparation or an algorithm acting on a finite encoding of \(\rho\); arbitrary complex matrix entries are allowed.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of existence of a single finite-dimensional state satisfying the NPT condition and every quantified rank-two inequality, or a complete Lean-checked proof of the logical negation: for every finite \(a,b\) and every NPT density matrix \(\rho\), some finite \(k\) and eligible unit vector \(\psi\) give a strictly negative expectation. In the second outcome, \(k\) and the vector may depend on \(\rho\), and no universal copy bound is requested. Numerical checks, one fixed copy count, a restricted set of test vectors, or a sequence of different states depending on \(k\) do not establish the existential all-copy statement. Positivity and negativity are exact; this yes/no problem has no numerical approximation substitute.
cards.why: A defining question about whether partial-transpose negativity completely captures the possibility of converting bipartite entanglement into useful Bell pairs. Its precise all-copy quantifier connects quantum resource theory to tensor-stable matrix inequalities.

cards.context:
Entanglement is a property of a state, whereas distillation is an operational ability to turn many noisy shared states into nearly perfect Bell pairs. These pairs are useful because a pair, together with classical communication, can transfer an unknown qubit by teleportation. The question asks whether there is a form of entanglement that passes the necessary negative-partial-transpose test for distillation but is nevertheless permanently unusable for this particular conversion.

The Horodeckis established that entangled states with positive partial transpose can be bound entangled. Their obstruction survives every tensor power: a positive semidefinite partial transpose remains positive semidefinite after tensoring, so no test vector can have negative expectation. This card concerns the complementary regime, where some negative eigenvector exists already, but its Schmidt rank may be too large to provide the rank-two witness needed for a distillation protocol.

In local dimension two, every bipartite vector has Schmidt rank at most two, so an NPT state is already one-copy distillable. The existence question therefore concerns larger local spaces. The formal statement still quantifies over all finite dimensions, with no promise that the state has a rational description, a symmetry, or an efficient preparation circuit.

DiVincenzo, Shor, Smolin, Terhal and Thapliyal investigated NPT states whose one-copy behavior differs from their spectral negativity. Their evidence did not establish one fixed NPT state undistillable for every finite number of copies. The present question retains that full order of quantifiers.

The Werner family is \(\rho_{\mathrm W}(d,\alpha)=(I+\alpha F)/(d^2+\alpha d)\), for \(d\ge2\) and \(-1\le\alpha\le1\), where \(F(u\otimes v)=v\otimes u\) swaps the two local systems and \(I\) is identity. Its members are NPT exactly for \(\alpha<-1/d\), and one-copy distillable exactly for \(\alpha<-1/2\). Thus \(-1/2\le\alpha<-1/d\) is the NPT one-copy-undistillable interval when \(d\ge3\). This is a known subclass; the target is not restricted to Werner states.

Several July 2026 papers prove that the one-copy and two-copy thresholds for Werner states coincide. Fraser and coauthors obtain this from a rank-constrained partial-trace inequality, with no Hermiticity or positivity assumption on the coefficient matrix. These results include the formerly open two-ququart example \(\rho _{\mathrm{W}}(4,- 1/2)\). They remove a major finite-copy obstacle, but do not prove that any particular NPT Werner state is undistillable for every number of copies.

Bharti, Gajjala and Haug also obtain the two-copy threshold and several restricted finite-copy extensions, while explicitly leaving the general all-copy assertion open. A family of states indexed by the allowed number of copies does not give the single fixed state required by the existential target.

Wu and Zou prove three-copy endpoint nonnegativity for specified sectors, including normal rank-two coefficient operators. A coefficient operator is the matrix of a bipartite test vector in product bases; normal means that the matrix commutes with its conjugate transpose. context_blocks.text: Entanglement is a property of a state, whereas distillation is an operational ability to turn many noisy shared states into nearly perfect Bell pairs. These pairs are useful because a pair, together with classical communication, can transfer an unknown qubit by teleportation. The question asks whether there is a form of entanglement that passes the necessary negative-partial-transpose test for distillation but is nevertheless permanently unusable for this particular conversion.

The Horodeckis established that entangled states with positive partial transpose can be bound entangled. Their obstruction survives every tensor power: a positive semidefinite partial transpose remains positive semidefinite after tensoring, so no test vector can have negative expectation. This card concerns the complementary regime, where some negative eigenvector exists already, but its Schmidt rank may be too large to provide the rank-two witness needed for a distillation protocol.

In local dimension two, every bipartite vector has Schmidt rank at most two, so an NPT state is already one-copy distillable. The existence question therefore concerns larger local spaces. The formal statement still quantifies over all finite dimensions, with no promise that the state has a rational description, a symmetry, or an efficient preparation circuit.

cards.title: Parity versus \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) with shallow quantum preprocessing
cards.formal: Does every polynomial-size constant-depth classical \(\mathrm{AC}^0\) circuit with polynomial-size constant-depth quantum preprocessing have asymptotically zero correlation with parity? Precisely, for every polynomial \(p\), constant \(d\in\mathbb N\), and sequence \((C_n,f_n)_{n\ge1}\) satisfying the model and bounds below, is \[\left|2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{0,1\}^n}\ \sum_{y\in\{0,1\}^{n+m(n)}}\Pr[C_n(x)=y]f_n(y)(-1)^{\sum_{i=1}^nx_i}\right|\longrightarrow0\quad(n\longrightarrow\infty)?\] Here \(m(n)\le p(n)\) zero-initialized ancillary qubits are allowed, both circuit stages have depth at most \(d\), and both have polynomial size bounded by \(p(n)\). There is no geometric locality, uniformity or clean-ancilla condition.
cards.definitions:
For \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\), parity in the sign convention is \(\operatorname{Par}_n(x)=(-1)^{x_1+\cdots+x_n}\). The quantum circuit \(C_n\) begins in the computational-basis state \(|x\rangle\otimes|0^{m(n)}\rangle\). A qubit is a two-dimensional complex Hilbert space, and the full register has state space \((\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes(n+m(n))}\). A gate is any unitary on one or two qubits, acting as identity on the others. Unitary means \(U^\dagger U=UU^\dagger=I\). Gates are arranged in layers, with disjoint supports in each layer. The number of layers is the quantum depth, at most \(d\); the total number of nonidentity gates is at most \(p(n)\). Any two wires may interact. The ancillary count is separately bounded by \(p(n)\), including ancillary wires that are only measured.

All output wires are measured once in the computational basis. If the product of the layers is \(U_n\), the resulting bit string \(y\) has probability \[\Pr[C_n(x)=y]=|\langle y|U_n|x,0^{m(n)}\rangle|^2.\] There are no intermediate measurements, adaptive gate choices or postselection. No ancillary wire has to return to zero, and garbage is allowed. The initial ancillas are zeros, not arbitrary input-dependent advice states. Gates may depend on \(n\) and may have arbitrary complex entries satisfying unitarity: this is the source's nonuniform circuit lower-bound model, not a uniform algorithm with free real-number input. Consequently no fixed finite gate alphabet or efficient gate-description requirement is imposed.

The classical postprocessor \(f_n:\{0,1\}^{n+m(n)}\to\{-1,1\}\) is a finite Boolean circuit of unbounded-fan-in AND and OR gates and fan-in-one NOT gates, with constants permitted. Its underlying output bit \(b\) is interpreted as \((-1)^b\). Classical depth is the greatest number of gates on an input-to-output path and is at most \(d\). Its number of gates is at most \(p(n)\); repeated identical incoming wires can be omitted. Including wires in the size instead gives an equivalent polynomial-size family, since the vertex count is polynomial. There are no parity gates, arbitrary Boolean lookup-table gates, threshold gates or extra classical advice inputs. The entire classical circuit is allowed to depend nonuniformly on \(n\).

The two stages are composed once: measure the quantum output, then apply the deterministic classical circuit to that outcome. The correlation is the expectation of \(f_n(Y)\operatorname{Par}_n(X)\) when \(X\) is uniform on all \(n\)-bit strings and, conditional on \(X=x\), \(Y\) follows the Born probabilities above. There is no promise on the input Hamming weight. The average success probability at computing sign parity is \((1+\operatorname{Corr}_n)/2\). Correlation is signed; the displayed limit of its absolute value is equivalent to the source's limit \(\operatorname{Corr}_n\to0\). It also rules out a persistent advantage after negating the output.

The polynomial, depth and circuit sequence are fixed before taking the limit, but are otherwise arbitrary. Equivalently, for each such choice and every real \(\varepsilon>0\), there must be an \(N\) such that \(|\operatorname{Corr}_n|<\varepsilon\) for all \(n\ge N\). No particular rate of decay is requested. A refutation can consist of one polynomially bounded sequence and one \(\varepsilon>0\) with \(|\operatorname{Corr}_n|\ge\varepsilon\) at infinitely many input lengths; constant correlation at every length is sufficient but is not necessary for a negative answer.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of the quantified zero-correlation limit, or a complete Lean-checked refutation under the same gate, ancilla, depth, size and average-input conventions. A positive result must allow every polynomially bounded number of zero ancillas and every polynomial-size classical postprocessor. Ancilla-free preprocessing, linear-size classical circuits, geometric restrictions, uniform families, a finite restricted gate set or a worst-case statement about one input do not cover the whole conjecture. A negative result must supply a circuit sequence with a proved failure of convergence; search or sampling advantages for another task do not suffice. This is an exact asymptotic proposition, not a request to estimate a correlation at finitely many sizes.
cards.why: Parity is a basic test of global information processing. Resolving this conjecture would show whether very shallow quantum preprocessing can give weak classical decision circuits a persistent advantage on a canonical Boolean function, beyond known quantum search and sampling separations.

cards.title: Log-rank conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,k\ge1\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\), for arbitrary nonempty finite sets X and Y, satisfies \(D(f)\le C\bigl(\log_2(r(f)+2)\bigr)^k\)? Here r(f) is the rank over the real numbers of its zero-one communication matrix, and D(f) is its exact deterministic communication complexity in bits.
cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and both know the complete function f, its finite domains and their chosen protocol. These shared data are not charged as communication. A protocol is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node specifies its sender and a function from that sender’s input set to \(\{0,1\}\). At that node the sender transmits this one bit, and both parties follow the corresponding edge; the node already records the preceding transcript. Every leaf is labeled 0 or 1. For every pair (x,y), the reached leaf must be labeled f(x,y), so both parties determine the exact answer. The cost is the maximum number of transmitted bits on any input pair, equivalently the tree depth after deleting unreachable branches. D(f) is the minimum cost among all correct trees; a finite protocol always exists. The protocol may depend arbitrarily on f, and its description length, local computation and number of communication rounds have no separate bound or charge. The communication matrix is \(M_f=(f(x,y))_{x\in X,y\in Y}\), treating its zeroes and ones as real scalars. Define \(r(f)=\operatorname{rank}_{\mathbb R}(M_f)\), the dimension of its column span over \(\mathbb R\). The particular enumeration of either domain does not matter. Rank zero means the all-zero function, which has D(f)=0, and the all-one function also has D(f)=0. The term r+2 avoids a zero or undefined logarithm at small ranks without changing the asymptotic conjecture. The same C and k must work for every choice of domains and function; the protocol need not be generated uniformly from the table. The statement has no promise pairs, missing matrix entries, distribution on inputs, randomness, quantum messages, approximation or one-way restriction. Rank over a finite field, approximate rank and sign rank are not the parameter used here. Some sources encode outputs by minus one and plus one. With \(A=2M_f-J\), where J is the all-one matrix, the two ordinary real ranks differ by at most one and the output relabeling does not change D(f); with the r+2 convention these formulations have the same polynomial-boundedness question. The explicit negation is: for every pair of integers C,k at least one, there exist nonempty finite X,Y and a total f such that \(D(f)>C(\log_2(r(f)+2))^k\). No effective generator of the counterexample functions is added.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of a single pair of universal constants C,k satisfying the displayed inequality, or prove its quantified negation excluding every such pair. An affirmative proof must apply to every total function in the exact interactive protocol model; it need not compute an optimal protocol efficiently. A negative proof must give arbitrarily strong failures of polynomial dependence on log-rank, with examples permitted to depend on C and k. Failure of one proposed exponent, a result for partial functions, or a bound using approximate rank, sign rank, randomness or quantum communication does not meet this target.
cards.why: One of the central organizing conjectures of communication complexity. It asks whether a basic linear-algebraic quantity characterizes efficient exact communication, and connects protocols to rectangle partitions, discrepancy, graph structure, and cancellation in matrix decompositions.

cards.context:
Matrix rank gives a general lower bound on communication. A protocol using at most d bits has at most \(2^{d}\) leaves, and the inputs reaching each leaf form a rectangle \(A\times B\). Summing the indicator matrices of the output-one rectangles represents \(M_{f}\) as a sum of at most \(2^{d}\) rank-one matrices. Consequently \(\log _{2}r(f)\le D(f)\) when \(r(f)\ge 1\). The conjecture asks whether this algebraic obstruction controls deterministic communication up to a polynomial.

An elementary upper bound goes in the other direction but is much larger. A rank-r Boolean matrix has at most 2ʳ distinct rows: choose r columns that determine every row, and record their Boolean entries. Alice can identify her row with at most r bits, after which Bob can determine the answer and send one output bit. This protocol makes clear why the question concerns the gap between rank and its logarithm.

A low-rank factorization permits arbitrary real coefficients and cancellation. A protocol instead needs a recursively organized partition into monochromatic rectangles. Moving between these kinds of structure is the main difficulty. Lovett used discrepancy to obtain an \(O(\sqrt{r} \log  r)\) communication bound; Sudakov and Tomon remove the logarithmic factor using a stronger discrepancy estimate for sparse matrices. The resulting \(O(\sqrt{r})\) remains far larger than a polynomial in log r.

Lower-bound constructions show that a linear bound in log-rank is too optimistic. Göös, Pitassi, and Watson obtain a nearly quadratic separation through query-to-communication lifting.

Song’s August 2026 preprint reports an explicit bound \(\Omega((\log r)^2/\log\log r)\) by refining the parameters in earlier constructions. This records the preprint’s stated result, whose proof and comparison of logarithmic losses were not independently verified here. In any event, a lower bound of this fixed polynomial order would not refute the conjecture, which permits a larger universal exponent.

Hambardzumyan, Lovett and Shirley prove that a rank-r Boolean matrix is a signed sum of \(O(r\log(r+2))\) rectangle indicator matrices. Their equivalent conjecture compares this with the minimum number of disjoint all-one rectangles that partition the one-entries. That one-sided partition number differs from both a partition of all entries into monochromatic rectangles and the leaves of a protocol tree. The equivalence is a proved reformulation, not an established bound for exact protocols.

A finite example disproving one proposed constant or exponent would still permit a different polynomial bound. A negative answer must exclude every universal polynomial, with the function and dimensions allowed to vary with that polynomial. A positive answer may choose a different protocol for each function; the conjecture imposes no efficient protocol-construction requirement.

cards.title: Exponential Time Hypothesis
cards.formal: Is \(s_3>0\) in the deterministic bit model defined below? Equivalently, does there exist one real \(c>0\) such that no 3-SAT decider A has a runtime bound \(t_A(F)\le C\,2^{c n(F)}(N(F)+1)^d\) on every valid 3-CNF formula F for any fixed integers \(C\ge1,d\ge0\)? The same positive c must exclude all such algorithms. This is the deterministic Exponential Time Hypothesis.
cards.definitions:
Use the shared [bounded-width CNF encoding and rate \(s_q\)](definitions.html#sat-encoding). The exponential term uses the number of distinct variables \(n(F)\). The polynomial factor uses the full input length \(N(F)\), including every repeated clause. The decider may depend on the fixed width \(q\).

This card specializes q to 3. Its negation, \(s_3=0\), means that for every real \(\varepsilon>0\) there is a 3-SAT decider \(A_\varepsilon\) with fixed constants \(C_\varepsilon,d_\varepsilon\) satisfying \(t_{A_\varepsilon}(F)\le C_\varepsilon 2^{\varepsilon n(F)}(N(F)+1)^{d_\varepsilon}\) on every valid formula. The machine and constants may depend on \(\varepsilon\). This statement does not require one machine with a single subexponential runtime bound, nor a computable map from \(\varepsilon\) to a machine.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof of \(s_3>0\) or of \(s_3=0\) for the explicitly defined rate. A positive answer requires a positive constant excluding every valid deterministic decider at that exponential rate, with any polynomial input factor. A negative answer must establish arbitrarily small attainable positive exponents with the stated quantifiers. A fixed improved positive exponent, a bound for a restricted algorithm class, or a conditional lower bound does not settle this question. No numerical estimate of \(s_3\) is requested: the target is its strict positivity.
cards.why: ETH is the central hypothesis for ruling out subexponential exact algorithms and many fixed-parameter speedups. It turns the qualitative P versus NP question into a quantitative claim that can be transferred through carefully sized reductions.

cards.context:
NP-completeness describes the possibility of polynomial-time algorithms and does not itself impose a positive exponential rate. Even if P differs from NP, a running time such as \(2^{\sqrt{n}}\) remains possible for 3-SAT. ETH asks for a stronger obstruction: some fixed amount of exponential work must remain unavoidable when complexity is measured by the number of Boolean choices.

That parameter must be preserved carefully by a reduction. An ordinary polynomial-time reduction may turn an n-variable formula into an instance of size \(n^{3}\), which can destroy a claimed exponential lower bound in the new parameter. Sparsification supplies a controlled disjunction of bounded-density formulas, allowing variables and clauses to be related without an arbitrary polynomial blowup. This is a main reason ETH can support sharp bounds across many problems.

The infimum over all algorithms matters. Excluding one \(2^{o(n)}\) algorithm is the common informal wording, but the textbook explicitly keeps the stronger positive-infimum statement because the converse is unclear. ETH would be false if arbitrarily small constant exponents were attainable, even if the known algorithms depended on the desired exponent. A card that omitted this distinction would change the quantified question.

Liu’s deterministic algorithm has runtime \(O(1.32793^n)\) up to polynomial input factors. It therefore supplies an upper bound on \(s_3\); it establishes neither a positive lower bound nor the value of \(s_3\). The existence of one algorithm with a positive exponential rate does not rule out a much faster algorithm. Empirical solver success and promises on the formula are also distinct from this all-input infimum.

ETH is weaker than SETH, whose optimal rates approach one as the fixed clause width grows. It also differs from randomized ETH and from Gap-ETH, which asks for hardness of distinguishing fully satisfiable formulas from formulas with a constant unsatisfied fraction. Recent lattice reductions illustrate the value of tracking these distinctions: some approximation hardness can be obtained from deterministic ETH, while other results use randomized ETH. They extend the consequences of assumptions without proving the assumptions.

A single fixed exponent in ETH must obstruct every algorithm. Refuting one proposed lower-bound constant does not suffice, because another smaller positive constant could still work. Conversely, a refutation may use a different finite algorithm for each desired exponent; no effective procedure generating those algorithms is added to the target.

cards.title: Near-optimal dimension dependence in bandit convex optimization
cards.formal: Do there exist universal constants \(C>0\) and \(a\in\mathbb N_0\) such that the one-point adversarial bandit convex-optimization minimax regret defined below satisfies \[R^*(d,T)\le C d\sqrt T\bigl(\log_2(d+T+2)\bigr)^a\qquad(d,T\in\mathbb N_{\ge1})?\] Losses take values in \([0,1]\), the adversary is oblivious, and the learner observes only the exact value of its current action. The guarantee is uniform over all normalized convex bodies in the stated model; no smoothness or computation-time restriction is imposed.
cards.definitions: Let \(d,T\ge 1\) be integers and \(B_{2}^{d}=\{x\in R^{d}:\sum_{i} x_{i}^{2}\le 1\}\). A permitted constraint set K is a compact convex subset of \(R^{d}\) satisfying \(B_{2}^{d}\subseteq K\subseteq dB_{2}^{d}\); the learner knows K,d,T in advance. This is an affine normalization of general full-dimensional convex bodies, not a smoothness condition on losses. Write \(F(K)\) for the Borel-measurable convex functions \(f:K\to [0,1]\), where convexity means \(f(\lambda x+(1- \lambda )y)\le \lambda f(x)+(1- \lambda )f(y)\) for \(x,y\in K\) and \(\lambda \in [0,1]\). No common Lipschitz, differentiability, strong-convexity or curvature bound is imposed. Before any play, an oblivious adversary fixes \(f_{1},\ldots ,f_{T}\in F(K)\), possibly using knowledge of the learner’s policy but not its realized random choices. At round t the learner chooses \(X_{t}\in K\), incurs \(f_{t}(X_{t})\), and observes exactly that one real value. It receives no noise, gradient, second evaluation, whole function or future loss. A policy is a sequence of Borel probability kernels assigning a distribution on K to each observed history \((X_{1},f_{1}(X_{1}),\ldots ,X_{t- 1},f_{t- 1}(X_{t- 1}))\). This permits arbitrary randomized decision rules; computation, representation and sampling time are unrestricted, so the target is statistical rather than polynomial-time optimization. For fixed K, define \(R_{K}(T)=\inf _{\pi} \sup _{f_{1},\ldots ,f_{T}} E_{\pi}[\sum_{t} f_{t}(X_{t})- \inf _{x\in K}\sum_{t} f_{t}(x)]\), with the supremum over fixed legal loss sequences and expectation only over policy randomness. Finally \(R*(d,T)=\sup _{K} R_{K}(T)\), over the normalized bodies above. The comparator is one fixed point for all rounds, chosen in hindsight. Using an infimum avoids assuming a minimizer on the boundary. The Borel convention ensures the displayed expectations are defined.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove in Lean that there are universal \(C,a\) giving the displayed regret upper bound for every \(d,T\), or prove that for every proposed pair the bound fails at some \(d,T\) in the stated one-point feedback model.

cards.context:
On the interval \([- 1,1]\), the convex losses \(f(x)=(1+x)/2\) and \(h(x)=(1- x)/2\) both equal \(1/2\) at \(x=0\), but their minimizing endpoints are opposite. Observing one loss value therefore need not reveal which way to move. Across rounds the loss may also change, so a value observed yesterday is not a second evaluation of today’s function.

Regret compares accumulated loss with the best single point that could have been used throughout the sequence. It does not compare with a different minimizer on every round. This distinction makes learning possible even when the environment changes. Randomization protects the learner against a sequence chosen before its random actions, while the adversary may still choose that sequence with knowledge of the policy.

Lattimore’s 2020 theorem gives an upper bound of order \(d^{5/2}\sqrt{T}\), apart from a logarithmic factor, for exact one-point feedback. In the regime where T is sufficiently large relative to d, known lower bounds grow as \(d\sqrt{T}\). The March 2026 book explicitly retains the dimension gap. For smaller horizons, regret is always at most T because each loss lies in \([0,1]\); an asymptotic expression must respect this saturation.

Bounded loss values fix the scale of regret. Restricting K to a rounded affine position prevents an arbitrary choice of coordinates from introducing an extra geometric parameter. This still permits general convex losses and many domain shapes. The information-theoretic question asks what is attainable by decision rules with no computation limit. A practical algorithm can be a major advance while still having a worse dimension dependence than the best existence bound.

The July 2026 revision of Ye’s paper uses two evaluations per loss and assumes strong convexity, with carefully stated comparator guarantees. Cheng, Hatano and Takimoto’s June 2026 result allows globally budgeted perturbations but assumes a smooth convex underlying loss even when the perturbations vanish. These assumptions differ from arbitrary bounded convex functions with one exact observation. Neither establishes the minimax rate requested here.

For the hard functions on the unit ball, \(f(0)=0\) and \(|f|\le1\). Set \(T=d^4\) and \(b=\sqrt{8\log(2T)}\). Draw independent standard Gaussians before play, truncate each by clipping to \([-b,b]\), and use the convex losses \(g_t(x)=1/2+(f(x)+\operatorname{clip}(Z_t,-b,b))/(2(1+b))\). These take values in \([0,1]\) and the offsets cancel against the fixed comparator. A learner on this exact feedback can be coupled to one in the source’s Gaussian model until the first clipped offset. Its probability is at most \(2T e^{-b^2/2}\), and the unscaled regret is at most \(2T\). The rescaling costs \(O(\sqrt{\log T})\). Averaging over offsets gives a fixed legal sequence attaining at least the average expected regret. At this polynomial horizon the dimension factor \(d^{1/4}\) dominates every fixed polylogarithm.

cards.title: Vertex reconstruction conjecture
cards.formal: For every integer \(n\ge 3\) and every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G,H on n vertices, does equality \(D(G)=D(H)\) of their vertex decks imply that G and H are isomorphic?
cards.definitions: A finite simple undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) has a finite vertex set V and an edge set E consisting of unordered two-element subsets of V; there are no loops or parallel edges. An isomorphism from G to H is a bijection \(f:V(G)\to V(H)\) such that \(\{u,v\}\) is an edge of G if and only if \(\{f(u),f(v)\}\) is an edge of H. Write \([G]\) for its isomorphism class. For \(v\in V(G), G- v\) is the induced graph on \(V(G)\setminus \{v\}\): remove v and exactly the edges incident with v. Define \(D(G)\) to be the multiset \(\{[G- v]:v\in V(G)\}\), with one entry for every deleted vertex. Thus \(D(G)=D(H)\) means that for each isomorphism class K of graphs on \(n- 1\) vertices, the number of vertices v with \([G- v]=K\) equals the corresponding number for H. Each entry forgets all original vertex labels, including the identity of the deleted vertex; repeated isomorphism classes retain their multiplicities. All graphs, including disconnected graphs and graphs with isolated vertices, are included. The question is a structural uniqueness statement and imposes no running-time requirement on an algorithm.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove that equal vertex decks imply isomorphism for every \(n\ge 3\), or refute the conjecture by exhibiting two nonisomorphic finite simple undirected graphs with \(n\ge 3\) and identical decks, with proofs of those properties.
cards.why: The conjecture asks whether all overlapping one-vertex views determine an entire graph. It tests how much structural information survives deletion and loss of labels, and connects graph structure to reconstruction and isomorphism problems.

cards.context:
Imagine receiving every graph obtained by deleting one vertex from an unknown graph, with the vertex labels erased in each view. Different deletions can yield identical-looking graphs, and their number of occurrences remains part of the data. The conjecture says this complete collection determines the original graph uniquely up to relabeling.

For a path on three vertices, deleting either endpoint leaves a single edge, while deleting the middle vertex leaves two isolated vertices. Its deck therefore consists of two copies of the edge and one edgeless two-vertex graph. The triangle instead has three copies of the edge. The lower limit of three vertices is necessary: an edge and an edgeless graph on two vertices both have a deck of two isolated single vertices.

Some global information survives deletion automatically. If \(n\ge 3\), every original edge appears in exactly \(n- 2\) members of the deck, so the total number of edges is the sum of the edge counts in the deck divided by \(n- 2\). Comparing each member’s edge count with that total also recovers the multiset of vertex degrees. These counts do not specify how all vertices fit together; that missing arrangement is the substance of the question.

Uniqueness has a different meaning from efficient recovery. There are finitely many graphs of a fixed order, so one can always enumerate those whose decks match the input. The conjecture says there is just one matching isomorphism class whenever the input is the deck of a graph with at least three vertices. It does not require that this enumeration be replaced by a polynomial-time algorithm.

McKay reports exhaustive verification through 13 vertices, and the 2026 revision by Heinrich and coauthors proves reconstruction for every interval graph with at least three vertices. Neither a finite range nor this particular graph class covers all finite graphs. The computations and proofs were not independently reproduced in this review.

A 2026 AI-assisted result concerns a structured bipartite incidence-deletion analogue: it retains the deleted vertex as an isolated vertex, preserves a given bipartition in isomorphisms, and assumes 2-connectivity and pairwise distinct vertex types. Its theorem is not the unrestricted vertex reconstruction conjecture.

The status record also preserves a 2024 general proof claim by O’Shea and Wilkins. Its publisher abstract was checked, but the full argument was inaccessible and is not validated here. Later specialist sources still formulate the general conjecture as open, so this review does not label it resolved.

cards.title: Linear-time directed shortest paths with nonnegative real weights
cards.formal: Do there exist an integer word-size constant \(B\ge3\), an absolute constant \(K>0\), and one uniform deterministic comparison-addition RAM algorithm that, on every explicitly given simple directed graph with \(n\ge2\) vertices and \(m\) arcs of arbitrary nonnegative real lengths, and every specified source vertex, outputs all exact source distances within \(K(n+m)\) instructions? The model below charges control, memory access, preprocessing and output as well as operations on real values.
cards.definitions:
The graph has vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), no loops and at most one arc for each ordered pair of distinct vertices; opposite arcs are allowed. Input consists of \(n,m\), a source \(s\in[n]\), and an arbitrary-order explicit list of all arcs, each with its two integer endpoints and one exact real length \(w_e\ge0\). There is no bound on real magnitudes or rationality. Zero lengths, zero-length cycles, disconnected graphs and vertices unreachable from the source are allowed.

A directed walk from \(s\) to \(v\) follows arcs in their given directions and has length equal to the sum of their lengths. The empty walk has length zero. For a reachable vertex, its distance is the minimum of these lengths; nonnegative weights allow repeated vertices to be removed without increasing length, so a minimum is attained by a simple path, or by the empty path when \(v=s\). An unreachable vertex has distance \(+\infty\). The output is an array indexed by \([n]\), containing each exact finite distance or a distinct infinity marker. No sorted order of distances is requested, and an unevaluated implicit distance expression is not the output.

The machine has integer control words of \(w=B\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil\) bits and separately typed exact-real cells. Integer addresses must fit a word. An instruction can read or write one cell, copy a value, compare values of the same type and branch. Integer instructions also include Boolean operations, logical shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^w\), and quotient or remainder by a nonzero word. A shift by at least \(w\) returns zero. Multiword computations pay for their constituent instructions.

Real instructions are copying, comparison, addition and subtraction, each of unit cost. Finitely many rational program constants are allowed. There is no real multiplication or division, rounding, floor, access to digits or bits, or conversion of an input-dependent real value to an integer. Real values cannot serve as addresses. Integer instructions cannot inspect real encodings. The saved subtraction convention can be represented with pairs of sums and comparisons of such pairs; it does not supply multiplication or encoding access. The infinity output is a separate tag and is not treated as a real operand.

One finite program and the constants \(B,K\) work for all \(n,m,s\), graphs and real inputs. There are no random bits, advice strings, precomputed input-dependent tables or free oracles. Every executed instruction counts, including graph preprocessing, initialization of working storage, control and address arithmetic, and writing the \(n\) outputs. Table construction is charged. Time is worst-case over all inputs, and includes every operation needed to choose the next real comparison or sum; bounding only the number of real arithmetic operations is insufficient. The algorithm must halt correctly on every allowed input. The linear bound is uniform over real edge values and graph density.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of existence of a program and constants with the stated all-input bound, or prove its logical negation in exactly this model. A one-sided improvement above linear time, a result only for undirected graphs or integer weights, or a bound that excludes control and preprocessing time does not suffice. A conditional lower bound establishes only its conditional conclusion unless the condition is also proved.
cards.why: An optimal linear algorithm would determine whether directed shortest paths with general nonnegative numerical lengths can be computed at the cost of reading the graph.

cards.title: Universal maximin-share approximation for additive goods
cards.area: Algorithmic game theory, mechanism design and fair division
cards.formal: Determine the universal maximin-share approximation constant for additive indivisible goods, \[\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}=\sup\bigl\{\alpha\in[0,1]:\ \forall n\ge1\ \forall m\ge0\ \forall v\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times m}\ \exists(A_1,\ldots,A_n)\in\Pi_n([m])\ \forall i\in[n],\ v_i(A_i)\ge\alpha\,\mu_i(v)\bigr\}.\] Here \(n,m\) range over integers, \(v_i(S)=\sum_{g\in S}v_{ig}\), and \(\mu_i(v)=\max_{(P_1,\ldots,P_n)\in\Pi_n([m])}\min_{j\in[n]}v_i(P_j)\). The benchmark asks for this one dimensionless constant with absolute error at most \(1/100\), together with a complete Lean-checked proof of the error bound.
cards.definitions: Write \([m]=\{1,\ldots,m\}\), with \([0]=\varnothing\). The set \(\Pi_n([m])\) consists of ordered \(n\)-tuples of pairwise disjoint subsets whose union is all of \([m]\); empty bundles are allowed. Each item belongs to exactly one agent, with no splitting, sharing, disposal, payments or externalities. Each entry \(v_{ig}\) is an arbitrary finite nonnegative real value, and values of bundles are additive. Every agent has the same entitlement; the number of agents determining each maximin share is the original \(n\). The partition maximizing \(\mu_i(v)\) is chosen separately for each agent using that agent’s valuations. Its maximum exists because there are finitely many partitions. If \(\mu_i(v)=0\), the corresponding approximation requirement is simply \(v_i(A_i)\ge0\); no ratio with a zero denominator is taken. Valuations need not be identical, normalized, strictly positive or drawn from a finite value set. The allocation may depend on the entire instance. No runtime bound, incentive condition, randomness model or finite encoding of the real entries is imposed, because the target concerns mathematical existence rather than efficient computation. The supremum is well-defined in \([0,1]\), since the feasible set contains zero. The question covers all finite agent and item counts simultaneously, rather than the best guarantee for any one fixed \(n\).
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a real number \(a\), or an unambiguous mathematical specification of one, and a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean that \(|a-\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}|\le1/100\), using exactly the universal domain and maximin-share definition above. A proved interval \([L,U]\) containing \(\alpha_{\mathrm{MMS}}\) with \(U-L\le1/50\) qualifies via its midpoint. One-sided guarantees, counterexamples without a matching sufficiently close lower bound, empirical searches, or results only for a fixed number of agents do not meet the criterion. Determination of the exact supremum is welcome but not required; the submitted approximation need not itself be a universally attainable allocation ratio. The existing gap between \(7/9\) and \(39/40\) is wider than the permitted interval.
cards.why: Maximin share gives each agent a fairness benchmark determined by their own values, independent of how the other agents evaluate the goods. These personal guarantees can conflict when objects are indivisible. The universal constant measures the unavoidable loss from satisfying all agents simultaneously, separating a limitation of fairness itself from a limitation of available algorithms. It is a central quantitative threshold for additive fair division, with significance across instances and arbitrary numbers of participants.

cards.title: Integer factorization in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Do there exist integers \(C\ge1,c\ge0\) and one uniform classical randomized algorithm A such that, for every positive integer N in binary, A outputs the complete prime factorization of N with probability at least \(2/3\), and for every random-bit sequence halts within \(C(n+1)^c\) bit steps, where \(n=\lfloor\log_2 N\rfloor+1\)? The same A, C and c must work for all N.
cards.definitions: The input is the ordinary base-two representation of N, with no leading zeroes; its length n counts bits, not the numerical value of N. The one-character string 1 represents N=1. The empty string and all strings beginning with 0 are invalid and must be rejected on every random-bit sequence within the same polynomial bound in their length. For \(N\ge2\), the unique correct factorization is the finite list \((p_1,e_1),\ldots,(p_r,e_r)\), where \(p_1<\cdots<p_r\) are primes, each \(e_i\) is a positive integer, and \(N=\prod_{i=1}^r p_i^{e_i}\). A prime is an integer at least 2 whose only positive divisors are 1 and itself. The correct list for N=1 is empty. To fix a binary output format, encode a nonnegative integer a by \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^b0\) followed by the b-bit binary representation of a+1, where \(b=\lfloor\log_2(a+1)\rfloor+1\). A successful output is 1 followed by code(r) and then code(p_i), code(e_i) for i in increasing order, with no other bits; the single bit 0 is the failure or invalid-input symbol. A is a probabilistic multitape Turing machine with one finite program, a fixed finite number of tapes and fixed finite alphabets. It has a read-only input tape and initially blank work and output tapes; a transition accesses only cells at the heads and moves each head by at most one cell. It may request one new independent fair bit at a transition. The probability space is \(\{0,1\}^{\mathbb N}\) with independent uniform coordinates, and the probability guarantee is separate for every fixed input N. The runtime is the total transition count, including all input access, random-bit requests, arithmetic and output writing. Every random-bit sequence obeys the clock; thus only finitely many random bits affect each run. A malformed factor list, an incorrect list and the failure symbol all count as failure on a positive input. The algorithm receives no promise that N is semiprime or belongs to a particular distribution, no advice or precomputed factors, no order-finding or factoring oracle, and no quantum or unit-cost operations on unbounded integers. The task is full factorization, not merely deciding whether N is prime.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete Lean-checked proof that one algorithm and constants satisfy the all-input success guarantee and the all-random-sequences polynomial clock, or prove that no such algorithm and constants exist. A negative proof must exclude arbitrary uniform classical randomized algorithms with arbitrary fixed polynomial exponents; excluding deterministic algorithms alone does not suffice. For the affirmative answer, correctness includes every prime base, multiplicity, ordering and product in the complete output. A heuristic complexity estimate, a guarantee for sampled or restricted inputs, or a quantum algorithm does not meet the stated classical worst-case target.
cards.why: Integer factorization is a basic inverse problem in arithmetic and a central test case for the potential power of quantum computation. Its classical complexity has direct consequences for factoring-based cryptography and for algorithms that currently require access to a factoring subroutine.

cards.context:
Multiplying the prime factors is easy, and the factors themselves fit in a polynomial-size output. Discovering them is the unresolved step. Trial division up to \(\sqrt{N}\) is polynomial in the number’s value but exponential in its binary input length. The distinction between N and log N is essential even when a newer algorithm improves the power of N substantially.

Primality testing and factorization are different tasks. The Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena algorithm decides in deterministic polynomial time whether a number is prime, without necessarily exhibiting a divisor when the answer is composite. It also makes a proposed full factorization efficiently checkable: verify that every listed base is prime and that the product is N.

Efficient verification makes the two common randomized formulations equivalent in existence: bounded-error polynomial worst-case time, and always-correct polynomial expected time with possible nontermination only on a probability-zero set of random tapes. This equivalence uses an all-input expected bound and fresh independent randomness, and the expected-time formulation alone does not give a worst-case clock on each run. The card chooses the bounded-clock formulation to state the success event without any runtime averaging.

The general number field sieve has the familiar heuristic expected-time estimate \(\exp (((64/9)^{1/3}+o(1))(\ln  N)^{1/3}(\ln  \ln  N)^{2/3})\). This is subexponential but still superpolynomial in the bit length. Rigorous deterministic bounds of \(N^{1/5+o(1)}\) make a different tradeoff and remain exponential in that length. Neither bound is a proof that faster classical factoring is impossible.

Shor’s quantum algorithm factors in polynomial time, using quantum order finding. It provides an upper bound in the quantum model and does not establish a classical lower bound.

The newer deterministic large-order theorem has a different output contract: it may produce a certified high-order group element instead of a divisor. Even when the requested order threshold is small and the subroutine is fast, that output alternative does not amount to a complete factorization. Its usefulness within factoring algorithms must not be mistaken for a solution of the entire factoring problem.

A classical polynomial-time factoring algorithm would undermine the corresponding cryptographic hardness assumptions. Neither the efficiency of multiplication nor a conjectured separation \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) provides a proved classical factoring lower bound. Factoring and inverting RSA are also distinct problems; the historical source explains that the reverse general reduction is unknown.

cards.title: Prime-field discrete logarithms in randomized polynomial time
cards.formal: Does there exist one uniform classical probabilistic multitape Turing machine \(A\), and integers \(C,c\ge1\), such that \(A\) halts within \(C(L+1)^c\) steps on every binary input of length \(L\) and every sequence of its random bits, and has the following correctness property? For every prime \(p\), every generator \(g\) of the multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), and every \(h\in\mathbb F_p^{\times}\), given the binary encoding of \((p,g,h)\) specified below, it outputs the unique integer \(x\in\{0,\ldots,p-2\}\) satisfying \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\) with probability at least \(2/3\).
cards.definitions: The field \(\mathbb F_p\) consists of residues \(\{0,\ldots,p-1\}\) with addition and multiplication modulo the prime \(p\). Its multiplicative group \(\mathbb F_p^{\times}\) is \(\{1,\ldots,p-1\}\) with multiplication modulo \(p\). The promise that \(g\) is a generator means that \(g^0,g^1,\ldots,g^{p-2}\), reduced modulo \(p\), list these \(p-1\) residues without repetition; hence the requested exponent exists and is unique. Each input integer is represented by its ordinary base-two expansion \(\operatorname{bin}(a)\), without leading zeros and with \(\operatorname{bin}(0)=0\). Writing \(\ell(a)=|\operatorname{bin}(a)|\), set \(\operatorname{code}(a)=1^{\ell(a)}0\operatorname{bin}(a)\). The complete input is \(\operatorname{code}(p)\operatorname{code}(g)\operatorname{code}(h)\), with \(p\) prime and \(1\le g,h<p\). Its length \(L=2(\ell(p)+\ell(g)+\ell(h))+3\) is \(\Theta(\log_2 p)\) on promised inputs. A successful output is exactly \(\operatorname{bin}(x)\); any different output or a designated failure symbol is unsuccessful. For \(p=2\), the sole promised pair is \(g=h=1\) and the answer is \(x=0\). The machine has a fixed finite program, fixed finite alphabets, a read-only input tape, finitely many work tapes and an output tape; each transition costs one step, and any random transition reads one fresh independent fair bit. The time bound includes input processing, bit arithmetic, random-bit generation, output and all preprocessing. The same \(A,C,c\) work for every input, with no advice, oracle, precomputed table or supplied factorization of \(p-1\). Arbitrary classical computations on the concrete binary residues are permitted, not just generic group operations. Malformed encodings may be rejected as failure; on well-formed triples outside the mathematical promise, only the global time bound is required. The success guarantee is separately for each promised triple, over the machine’s coins, not over a distribution of primes or targets. The question concerns the multiplicative group of a prime field; additive groups, extension fields and elliptic-curve groups are different models.
cards.answer_criterion: Supply a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of existence of \(A,C,c\) with both the all-input, all-random-sequence time bound and the per-promised-input success guarantee, or a Lean-checked proof that no such triple exists. Equivalently, a negative answer must prove that every machine obeying some global polynomial clock has a promised input on which its probability of outputting the required exponent is less than \(2/3\). Failure of a particular algorithm, an average-case conjecture for a selected prime distribution, or a lower bound restricted to generic group operations does not establish this negation. A quantum algorithm, success only for selected prime families, or a bound polynomial in \(p\) rather than its bit length does not meet the positive target.
cards.why: Discrete logarithms expose a basic gap between efficient modular exponentiation and our ability to invert it. A uniform classical polynomial-time solver would defeat the corresponding finite-field discrete-logarithm assumptions and solve computational Diffie–Hellman in this setting. An unrestricted impossibility proof would establish a fundamental classical lower bound for a concrete arithmetic problem already solvable in quantum polynomial time.

cards.context:
For a supplied \(g\) and exponent \(x\), modular exponentiation takes time polynomial in their bit lengths. Inverting this operation would reveal the shared value \(g^{ab}\) from \(g,g^a,g^b\) in the corresponding Diffie–Hellman setting. This implication does not identify discrete-logarithm hardness with every Diffie–Hellman or encryption-security assumption. The card asks a worst-case algorithmic question; a negative answer alone does not prove average-case hardness for a cryptographic parameter distribution.

Candidate answers are efficiently verifiable by checking \(0\le x\le p-2\) and \(g^x\equiv h\pmod p\). Thus, as an elementary consequence of verification, existence of the stated bounded-error algorithm is equivalent to existence of a Las Vegas solver that is never wrong and has a uniform polynomial expected running-time bound on every promised input. Independent verified repetition has bounded expected cost in one direction; truncation at three times an expected-time bound gives success at least \(2/3\) by Markov’s inequality in the other. This does not require every run of a Las Vegas solver to terminate, only probability-one termination and finite expected cost.

Schirokauer’s survey gives a conjectured expected-time NFS bound of the form \(\exp(O((\ln p)^{1/3}(\ln\ln p)^{2/3}))\) in the prime-field regime. This is a heuristic complexity analysis, not an unconditional polynomial-time theorem or an unrestricted lower bound. The displayed scale grows faster than every fixed power of \(\log p\). The 2024 Discrete Logarithm Factory paper separately studies costs shared across fields and targets; any such preprocessing must still fit this card’s complete single-input budget.

Shoup’s lower bound concerns randomly encoded group elements. If \(q\) is the largest prime divisor of a cyclic group’s order, constant success requires \(\Omega(\sqrt q)\) generic group operations in that model. His parameter \(q\) is not the field characteristic \(p\); for this card the group order is \(p-1\). The theorem averages over the random encoding, exponent and algorithm coins. It does not exclude algorithms that use the actual integer residues and their arithmetic structure.

Kleinjung and Wesolowski’s Theorem 1.1 gives expected time \((p d)^{2\log_2 d+O(1)}\) for the multiplicative group of \(\mathbb F_{p^d}\). For fixed \(p\) and growing extension degree \(d\), this is quasipolynomial in the input size. Substituting \(d=1\) supplies at most a polynomial-in-\(p\) guarantee, not the requested polynomial in \(\log p\). The occurrence of the product \(p d\) in their bound must not be confused with the field order \(p^d\).

Lido’s paper, published in March 2026, also proves a quasipolynomial expected-time theorem in small characteristic. In the inspected version its hypothesis is explicitly \(d>p\) for a field of size \(p^d\), excluding the growing prime-field family with \(d=1\). The source’s field-regime restriction remains part of the theorem even though all these problems share the name discrete logarithm.

Shor’s polynomial-time algorithm uses quantum computation. Wu and coauthors’ August 2026 preprint uses the same prime-field generator-input problem as an explicit classical-hardness assumption for a claim about estimating outputs of adaptive shallow quantum circuits. That assumption is not a proved classical lower bound; the reduction and its quantum resource claims were not independently verified in this review.

cards.why: Tree codes protect communication whose later symbols depend on earlier interaction. A constant alphabet and positive tree distance would keep redundancy bounded while maintaining distinguishability after every possible divergence. Efficient deterministic encoding and decoding would supply a central explicit object in the theory of reliable interactive communication.

cards.title: Finite-domain promise CSP dichotomy
cards.formal: For every fixed pair of finite relational structures \(A,B\) of the same finite signature, with nonempty domains and a homomorphism \(A\to B\), is the decision promise problem \(\operatorname{PCSP}(A,B)\) either solvable by a uniform deterministic polynomial-time algorithm or NP-hard under deterministic polynomial-time many-one promise reductions? Its yes instances are the finite structures \(I\) with \(I\to A\); its no instances are those with \(I\not\to B\). The quantifier ranges over all finite signatures and template pairs. The algorithm or hardness reduction, including its polynomial bound, may depend on the fixed pair.
cards.definitions:
A signature is an ordered finite list \(R_1,\ldots,R_s\), where \(s\geq0\) and each symbol has a fixed positive integer arity \(r_i\). A finite structure \(D\) for this signature has a finite domain and relations \(R_i^D\subseteq D^{r_i}\). The templates have domains \(A=\{1,\ldots,a\}\), \(B=\{1,\ldots,b\}\) for positive integers \(a,b\); their relation tables are fixed, not part of the varying input. Different template domains are allowed. For two structures of the same signature, a homomorphism \(h:D\to E\) is a map of domains satisfying
\[\forall i\;\forall(v_1,\ldots,v_{r_i})\in R_i^D:\ (h(v_1),\ldots,h(v_{r_i}))\in R_i^E.\]
Write \(D\to E\) if such a map exists, and \(D\not\to E\) if none exists. Homomorphisms need not be injective. Empty relations and repeated coordinates in a tuple are allowed.

An input structure \(I\) has domain \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\geq0\), and explicitly listed relation tuples. Fix the following binary encoding. Write \(n\) as the unary prefix \(1^n0\). In signature order, write the number \(t_i\) of listed tuples of relation \(i\) as \(1^{t_i}0\), followed by its tuples in their listed order. Encode each coordinate \(v\) by \(1^{|w|}0w\), where \(w\) is the binary expansion of \(v\) without leading zeros and \(1\leq v\leq n\). Each tuple has exactly \(r_i\) coordinates. Duplicate tuples are permitted in the encoding and denote the same relation member; their bits still count. The input ends after the last relation list, with no trailing bits. Thus \(L\), the length of the entire encoding, accounts for the domain as well as all constraints. The empty-domain structure is valid only with all lists empty and is a yes instance. Any encoding polynomial-time equivalent to this explicit representation gives the same question.

For a fixed pair, define \(Y_{A,B}=\{I:I\to A\}\) and \(N_{A,B}=\{I:I\not\to B\}\). The assumption \(A\to B\) makes these sets disjoint. A valid decision algorithm accepts every input in \(Y_{A,B}\) and rejects every input in \(N_{A,B}\). It may give either answer when \(I\to B\) but \(I\not\to A\). Polynomial time means a single deterministic multitape Turing machine with a finite program, no advice or oracle, halting on every binary input of length \(L\) within \(C(L+1)^k\) steps for some fixed positive integers \(C,k\). It returns reject on malformed encodings; even instances outside the promise must obey the time bound. Reading, writing and manipulating bits all count. The constants and machine may depend on \(A,B\) and their signature, but not on \(I\).

NP-hardness here means that one uniform deterministic polynomial-time map sends every 3-CNF formula \(\varphi\) to a valid input structure \(I_\varphi\) and satisfies
\[\varphi\text{ satisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\to A,\qquad
\varphi\text{ unsatisfiable}\Rightarrow I_\varphi\not\to B.\]
A 3-CNF formula is a finite conjunction of clauses, each the disjunction of three signed Boolean variables; repeated variables and literals are allowed. For definiteness, encode its number of clauses in unary followed by three literals per clause, each a sign bit and a positive variable index encoded by the same length-prefixed binary convention as coordinates above. A positive literal is true when its variable is 1, and a negative literal when its variable is 0. The reduction's bound is polynomial in the entire formula encoding, including the time and bits needed to output \(I_\varphi\). Malformed formula encodings may map to the empty input structure. Both satisfiable and unsatisfiable formulas must map into the promise.

The question is the inclusive disjunction of these two possibilities for each fixed pair; it assumes neither \(\mathrm{P}\ne\mathrm{NP}\) nor that the alternatives are disjoint. It does not request an algorithm that, given template tables, identifies the alternative, nor a common polynomial bound over all pairs. Producing a \(B\)-valued homomorphism on every input promised to map to \(A\) is the separate search task. Counting assignments, weighted objectives, allowing a fraction of violated constraints and robustness to broken promises are not part of this decision problem.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete, mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated dichotomy for every fixed finite pair, or of its logical negation. A negative answer must establish a fixed finite signature and pair \(A\to B\) whose decision promise problem admits neither any qualifying deterministic polynomial-time decider nor any qualifying polynomial-time many-one reduction from 3-SAT. Both failures must be proved; a presently unclassified pair is not a counterexample. The positive answer need not effectively classify templates, but must establish the full quantified disjunction without an unproved complexity assumption. A dichotomy only for a restricted family, a conditional general classification, or a theorem only about the search task does not settle this target.
cards.why: This asks whether finite local constraint descriptions force a sharp complexity classification even when the accepted and rejected instances are separated by a promise. It encompasses approximate graph colouring and many relaxed feasibility problems. A resolution would determine whether the organizing principle of the finite CSP dichotomy extends beyond exact satisfaction, or whether a fixed finite promise can have intermediate decision complexity.

references.authors: Joshua Brakensiek, Venkatesan Guruswami, Marcin Kozik and Xuandi Ren
references.locator: Direct reduction from 3-SAT and dichotomies for digraphs without sources or sinks and for Boolean templates with unate polymorphisms.

cards.context:
A promise CSP uses a stronger and a weaker version of each local requirement. For fixed integers \(2\leq k\leq c\), the templates \(A=K_k\) and \(B=K_c\), with the inequality edge relation, distinguish graphs that admit a proper \(k\)-colouring from graphs that admit no proper \(c\)-colouring. A proper colouring assigns different colours to adjacent vertices. Instances between these two cases impose no answer requirement. This is a qualitative relaxation of every constraint, rather than an objective to maximize the number satisfied.

For \(A=B\), there is no gap between the two cases. Bulatov and Zhuk independently established the finite-template CSP dichotomy in 2017: every such exact satisfaction problem is polynomial-time solvable or NP-complete. Classifying the two endpoint CSPs separately does not classify the promise problem, because the weaker required answer can make it easier than either endpoint.

One concrete polynomial-time example has Boolean domains, the stronger ternary relation \(\{(1,0,0),(0,1,0),(0,0,1)\}\), and the weaker relation \(\{0,1\}^3\setminus\{(0,0,0),(1,1,1)\}\). Thus it relaxes exactly-one satisfaction to not-all-equal satisfaction. Barto proves that every finite intermediate template \(C\) with \(A\to C\to B\) has an NP-complete exact CSP. Consequently this tractable promise pair has no tractable finite intermediate CSP unless \(\mathrm{P}=\mathrm{NP}\).

A \(q\)-ary polymorphism of a pair is a function \(p:A^q\to B\) that sends any \(q\) tuples of each \(R_i^A\), applied coordinate by coordinate, to a tuple of \(R_i^B\). Here \(q\geq1\). This describes operations that combine stronger solutions into a weaker solution. Unlike operations on a single domain, these maps do not generally allow unrestricted self-composition. This distinction helps explain why the classical classification does not directly extend to promises.

Brakensiek and Guruswami obtained a dichotomy for symmetric Boolean promise languages with negations. Ficak, Kozik, Olšák and Stankiewicz subsequently removed that extra requirement and classified all symmetric Boolean pairs: both domains are Boolean and every relation is unchanged under permuting its coordinates. Symmetry remains a substantive restriction; this does not classify arbitrary Boolean relations or arbitrary finite domains.

A 2026 theorem settles another restricted family. Let \(\mathrm{LO}_d\) have domain \(\{0,\ldots,d-1\}\) and the ternary relation consisting of triples whose maximum occurs exactly once. In particular, \(\mathrm{LO}_2\) is the exactly-one Boolean template. Krokhin and Vagnozzi prove that \(\operatorname{PCSP}(\mathrm{LO}_2,\mathrm{LO}_3)\) is NP-hard. Their Corollary 2 classifies every three-element target \(B\) with a single symmetric ternary relation and \(\mathrm{LO}_2\to B\): it is NP-hard if \(B\to\mathrm{LO}_3\), and polynomial-time solvable otherwise. Their hardness concerns the decision promise as well as search.

Banakh, Barsukov and Nakajima relate a logical class called Promise MMSNP to finite-domain promise CSPs. Their 2026 monochromatic-clique classification concerns a specified family and relies on the Rich 2-to-1 Conjecture for its hardness direction. Neither the general logical correspondence nor that conditional family theorem supplies an unconditional dichotomy for all finite pairs.

The 2022 survey explicitly treats a general dichotomy as a question with insufficient evidence for a consensus conjecture. The published ICALP 2026 article makes the same distinction while resolving its own restricted family. Decision and search must also remain separate: the article states that their general polynomial-time equivalence is not known. The present card asks only for the fixed-template decision dichotomy.
